opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at that point I didn't really have offers I felt excited about. I'd applied to a number of programs in the US, and the responses I was getting were either rejections or nothing at all. There were maybe one or two possibilities, but they weren't in the direction I really wanted. I was already quite sure I wanted to do computer vision and machine learning, and the options I had didn't feel like they'd let me do that seriously.

So it was a pretty anxious period. As an undergrad in China back then, you don't have much of a network. You send emails to professors, you read their papers, you try to write something thoughtful, and most of the time you just don't hear back. You start to doubt yourself and wonder whether you're aiming too high, or whether you should settle for something safer.

When Zhuowen replied, it felt very different. It wasn't just "yes, here's a spot." It felt like someone had actually looked at what I'd done and thought there was something there. That mattered a lot to me. Looking back, I think it was one of those moments where a single person's willingness to take a chance on you changes your whole trajectory. Before that, I was mostly just hoping something would work out. After that, I felt I had a real starting point.

r001.rationale: The response says his available options did not fit his computer vision and machine learning interests, but it does not attribute his frustration specifically to lacking an offer from a computer-vision professor he wanted to work with.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I wasn't that excited about them. I had a few offers, and on paper they were fine schools, good programs. But none of them felt right. The problem was that I didn't really have a clear picture of what I wanted to work on. I knew I was interested in vision, in learning, but I couldn't point to a specific advisor and say, this is the person whose problems I want to spend five years thinking about.

So I was in this strange state. I was supposed to be happy, right? You get into a PhD program, you should celebrate. But I remember feeling kind of hollow about it, like I was about to make a very important decision mostly by default, just because the deadline was approaching.

I had actually emailed Zhuowen earlier, because I had read some of his papers and his way of thinking about problems, especially the connection between vision and learning, really resonated with me. But he didn't reply for a long time. I had basically given up. I assumed he wasn't taking students or just wasn't interested.

Then quite late in the process, he wrote back. And the moment I read that email, I knew. It wasn't a rational comparison of rankings or funding. It was just a feeling that this is the person I want to learn from. Looking back, I think that early uncertainty was actually useful. It taught me that in research, choosing the right person to work with matters far more than choosing the right institution.

r001.rationale: He says his existing offers felt hollow because he lacked an advisor whose work he wanted to pursue, then explains that Zhuowen—whose vision and learning research resonated with him—had not replied until late in the process.

astra-6.text: I felt encouraged to have those offers, but I was still weighing my options. I hadn’t reached the point where I felt sure about where I wanted to go.

r001.rationale: The response says he felt encouraged but was still weighing options; it does not attribute frustration to the absence of an offer from a desired computer-vision professor.

sol-6.1.text: I felt relieved to have some options, but I was still unsure which one would be the right fit. Getting an offer is exciting, of course, but choosing where to spend the next several years is a different question. So before Professor Tu replied, I hadn’t really made up my mind.

r001.rationale: The response says he felt relieved to have options and was unsure which was the right fit. It does not attribute frustration to lacking an offer from a computer-vision professor he wanted to work with.
